title: Serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling & runbooks
author: Jordan Lee
body:
Overview

This page consolidates the serving runtime team wiki: runtime architecture, kernel scheduling guidance, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite instructions, release notes checklist, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is intended as the single source of truth for engineering and SRE teams managing Redwood's inference runtime.

Summary and intent

- Purpose: Document how the serving runtime is organized, how kernel selection and scheduling are configured, standard profiling workflows, benchmark procedures, recent release notes, and ops runbooks for incident response.
- Audience: runtime engineers, platform SREs, performance engineers, and on-call responders.
- Scope: production and pre-prod clusters (hosted and Dedicated), including GPU fleet config and private deployment considerations.

1) Runtime architecture (high-level)

Intro
The serving runtime is a modular, GPU-optimized inference engine layered with an orchestration control plane. Key modules: request router, scheduler, model-worker (executor), KV cache manager, telemetry/telemetry-exporter, and fallback/variant manager.

Architecture diagram (textual)
- API Layer (ingress): rate-limiter, auth, request validation
- Router: policy-based routing (latency/cost/region/customer-tier)
- Scheduler: job queue, batching windows, kernel selector
- Executors (Model workers): model shards, KV cache, attention kernels, quantized execution paths
- Observability: prometheus exporters, p99 tracing, per-token cost metrics
- Control plane: model registry, rollout manager, autoscaling policies

Ownership and services
- service/runtime-router: team runtime-router (owner: @runtime-router)
- service/runtime-scheduler: team serving-runtime (owner: @serving-runtime)
- service/model-executor: team model-serving (owner: @model-serving)
- telemetry/exporter: eng-platform (owner: @eng-platform)

SLOs and objectives
- 99th percentile generation latency (1k tokens): <= 1200ms (hosted), <= 1000ms (dedicated)
- Mean tokens/sec per-GPU (NVIDIA H100-80GB): baseline 140 tokens/sec for gpt-like 7B FP16 under default kernel selection
- Request success rate (4xx/5xx): >= 99.99%

2) Kernel selection and scheduling

Principles
- Select kernels by model architecture + sequence length distribution + batch size to maximize utilization and minimize tail latency.
- Prefer fused attention and attention-cache-aware kernels for generation workloads.
- Maintain deterministic fallbacks for unsupported operators (explicit mapping table in model-registry).

Kernel table (example)
| Model family | Preferred kernel | Conditions |
|--------------|------------------|------------|
| Transformer-gpt-arch | fused-attn-v3 | seq_len <= 2048, batch <= 16 |
| MLP-heavy | tile-matmul | dense only, fp16|
| Llama2-like | kv-cache-optimized | autoregressive workloads |

Scheduler modes
- latency_slo (default for hosted): tight batching window (5ms), preemptive short jobs, conservative dynamic batching thresholds
- throughput_cost (default for Dedicated cost-savings): longer batching window (25ms), aggressive packing across requests, GPU pooling enabled
- private_deployment: configurable per-customer policy file in /etc/redwood/runtime-policy.yaml

Tuning knobs (config file excerpt)
```
# /etc/redwood/runtime-policy.yaml
scheduler:
  mode: latency_slo
  max_batch_size: 32
  batching_window_ms: 5
  preemption_threshold_ms: 150
kernel_selection:
  prioritized_kernels: ["fused-attn-v3","kv-cache-optimized","tile-matmul"]
```

3) Profiling playbook (how to profile and triage perf regressions)

Goal: produce repeatable profiles that isolate CPU/GPU/memory/PCIe bottlenecks and attribute to kernel selection, batching, or model changes.

Pre-steps
1. Reproduce: use the benchmark harness (see section 4) to reproduce workload and collect baseline.
2. Tag: create a profiling tag in telemetry (profile_id: team/issue/timestamp).

Profiling steps
1. Collect runtime metrics (live):
   - prometheus query: rate(runtime_request_count[5m]) by (model, kernel)
   - p99 latency: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(runtime_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le))
2. Capture GPU-level counters:
   - nvidia-smi dmon -s u -d 0.5 -o DT
   - nsight systems: nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx -o /tmp/profile
3. Collect per-thread CPU profiles (Flamegraphs):
   - perf record -F 99 -g -p <pid> -o perf.data
   - perf script | FlameGraph/stackcollapse-perf.pl | FlameGraph/flamegraph.pl > flame.svg
4. Kernel-level time breakdown (sample):
   - Enable runtime debug histograms: POST /internal/debug/metrics?histograms=1
   - Look for large kernel execution time and heavy memcpy (H2D/D2H) patterns.

Common triage checklist
- High memcpy times -> check pinned memory settings and batching alignment.
- High kernel queueing -> check scheduler batching window or oversubscription.
- Spikes in CPU scheduling -> ensure background GC/maintenance tasks are throttled on serving nodes.

4) Benchmarking suite (how to run and interpret)

Location: git repo infra/benchmarks/serving-harness (branch: main). The suite supports deterministic replay of production traces and synthetic generation loads.

Quickstart (local emulated GPU)
1. Clone repo and set up docker images: ./scripts/build-images.sh
2. Run harness: ./scripts/run-benchmark.sh --model llama2-7b --seq 1024 --concurrency 20 --duration 300
3. Output: results/<timestamp>/report.json and perf/<timestamp>/{nsys,profiling,metrics}.

Key metrics reported
- tokens/sec (aggregate and per-GPU)
- p50/p90/p99 latency for generation and warm-start
- GPU utilization and power draw
- memory high-water marks and OOM count

Interpreting results
- Use baseline file (benchmarks/baselines/<model>-baseline.json) to compare regression. Example alert rule: if p99 latency > baseline_p99 * 1.25 -> create regression ticket.

5) Release notes checklist (runtime releases)

For every runtime release: release notes must include:
- Summary of changes (kernel updates, new heuristics, bug fixes)
- Performance impact: before/after tokens/sec and p99 latency for standard models (Llama2-7B, GPT-4-mini if applicable)
- Rollout plan: canary percentage, monitoring checks, rollback criteria
- Migration steps for Dedicated/private customers (config file diffs)

Template (example)
- Release: serving-runtime v2028.09.3
- Highlights: fused-attn-v3 enabled by default for Llama2 family; memory leak fixed in KV cache patch #487
- Benchmarks: Llama2-7B p99 -10% (improved), throughput +8% on H100
- Rollout: 5% canary -> 25% -> 100% with 30m observation windows; abort if 5xx increases > 0.1% or p99 regresses > 15%

6) Known issues (active and historical)

- Issue: intermittent kernel fallback for fused-attn-v3 on older CUDA drivers (observed on Ubuntu 20.04 with driver 520.x)
  - Impact: small subset of Dedicated hosts fall back to slower kernel, causing p99 latency spike
  - Mitigation: pin drivers to 535+ for affected hosts; temporary policy: scheduler.force_kernel=fallback
- Issue: KV cache memory fragmentation leading to OOM on long-lived sessions (>24h)
  - Impact: rare OOMs on high-concurrency customers
  - Mitigation: scheduled cache compaction task (see runbook) and restart policy with graceful evict
- Issue: preemption can cause short-lived tail spikes when mixing long/short requests
  - Mitigation: prefer latency_slo mode for mixed workloads; update request classification heuristics (PR #612)

7) Runtime runbooks (operational procedures)

Runbook A: High p99 latency for model X
1. Confirm: Check dashboards/runtime/model-X/latency (p99 > target)
2. Identify scope: is it single node, AZ, or global? (use routers by region)
3. Profile a sample request with sampling rate 1% (endpoint: /internal/trace/attach)
4. If kernel queueing observed: increase batching_window_ms by 2x on affected pool and monitor for 10 minutes
5. If memory OOMs: add nodes to pool and enable eviction (control plane: /api/v1/pools/<id>/eviction)
6. If regression persists: failover route to compatible model variant (model-registry suggests nfallback) and open incident.

Runbook B: Node-level GPU OOMs
1. Drain node from load: kubectl cordon/evict or autoscaling action
2. Collect logs: /var/log/runtime-executor.log, nvml logs, dmesg
3. Trigger cache compaction: curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/internal/cache/compact
4. Reintroduce node after memory stabilizes; if OOMs reoccur, collect heapdump and create bug (runtime-team)

Escalation matrix
- Pager: runtime-oncall -> primary SRE (30m) -> on-call eng lead (60m) -> exec notif (4h)
- Slack channels: #runtime-ops, #incident-response

8) Team wiki and knowledge pointers

Permanent links and resources
- Model registry: git+https://git.internal/redwood/model-registry
- Benchmark harness: git+https://git.internal/redwood/infra/benchmarks/serving-harness
- Kernel catalog: /docs/kernel-catalog.md (internal)
- Observability dashboards: Grafana -> Redwood / Runtime / Models

Best practices and conventions
- Always include before/after benchmark numbers in PR when changing kernels or scheduler defaults.
- Use standardized profiling tag format: runtime.profile.<team>.<issue>.<YYYYMMDD-HHMM>
- For private deployments, include a short compatibility matrix in PRs for supported CUDA/drivers/OS versions.

Appendix: Common commands and snippets

Prometheus queries
- p99 latency (5m window): histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(runtime_request_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le))
- tokens/sec by model: sum(rate(runtime_tokens_generated[1m])) by (model)

nsys example
- nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt -o /tmp/nsys-profile --sample=cpu --duration=120s --capture-range=nvtx

perf + flamegraph flow
- perf record -F 99 -g -p <pid> -o perf.data
- perf script | ./stackcollapse-perf.pl | ./flamegraph.pl > /tmp/flame.svg

Config locations
- Runtime policy: /etc/redwood/runtime-policy.yaml
- Kernel registry: /var/lib/redwood/kernel-catalog.json
- Executor logs: /var/log/runtime-executor.log

Contact and ownership
- Primary owner: serving-runtime team (team alias: @serving-runtime)
- On-call rotation: see PagerDuty schedule (link: https://pagerduty.internal/redwood/rotations/runtime)
- For release coordination: contact release-manager@redwood.com
